Turn Google Drive into a Network Drive Using Rclone

Did you ever wonder if you can setup your Google drive as a directory on your Linux file server so all of your other devices can see it as…
David Vasquez
a11y-light · September 30, 2025 (Updated: September 30, 2025) · Free: No

Did you ever wonder if you can setup your Google drive as a directory on your Linux file server so all of your other devices can see it as a network location?

Well, wonder no more, because you definitely can achieve this with rclone!

Here's my scenario. As you may have seen in my other articles, I built a budget Linux server to run various services and it has been working very well. However, since this was a budget build I found myself not having much room on this machine.

I was curious one day and wanted to see if I could utilize what I already had before thinking about purchasing more hard drives, my cloud services.

I have a Google subscription that comes with extra Drive storage (2TB), and OneDrive for my business that also comes with 1TB.

That's a lot of storage. "Can I use this?" I asked myself. The goal was to connect my cloud services to my Linux machine, so that my Windows devices on my network can see it as a shared network folder. I can achieve exactly that with rclone! Let me show you how.

What is rclone?

Rclone is a super helpful tool for managing files across cloud storage services, like Google Drive and Microsoft's OneDrive. On a Linux server, it can connect to Google Drive so you can sync files, perform backups, or even mount your Drive as a network filesystem, which we will be doing here. This makes it easy to access and manage Google Drive data directly from your server, and can alleviate storage on your devices by using it as a network drive.

Installation

Ok, so open up a terminal on your Linux machine, or SSH into it if accessing remotely. The first thing we're going to do is to install rclone.

Enter in the following commands:

sudo apt update

curl https://rclone.org/install.sh | sudo bash

That's pretty much the setup there. We're also going to use Samba. To learn more about Samba, take a look at this story here:

Setting Up a Home File Server

Enter this here to install Samba:

sudo apt install samba

Configuration

Alright, we got the installations out of the way, let's move on to the configuration. First, we're going to start the interactive setup. To begin, enter this command:

rclone config

For the interactive setup, follow the procedure below:

  • New remote: Press n.
  • Name: Enter a name for your remote. In my case, I named it gdrive2.
  • Storage: You will get a list of different storage types. For Google Drive, type drive or the number beside it. Since the numbers can vary, it's simple just to type drive but it doesn't matter either way, as long as it's the correct number.
  • client_id / client_secret: Leave both blank (press Enter).
  • scope: Choose 1 for full access. Like storage, you can also type drive.
  • root_folder_id / service_account_file: Leave both blank (press Enter).
  • Edit advanced config?: Press n for No.
  • Use auto config?: Press y for if you are on your Linux machine directly. Enter n if you are doing this remotely via SSH.
  • Authorize: A browser window will appear automatically if you are on your Linux machine directly. If you are on a remote computer, copy the verification code from the browser, and paste it into the terminal.
  • Configure as a Shared Drive?: Press n for No.

Ok, that's it for the interactive setup. You'll be taken to the first screen and you should see your new remote. I have my gdrive that already existed, but now my gdrive2 is showing up as well. Press n to quit the setup.

Let's do a little test to make sure that it's working. If you run the 'rclone mkdir REMOTE_NAME' command, you can create a new directory on your Google Drive. Here's what mine looks like:

Ok, so as per this command, I should see a folder in my Google drive called 'meowtest1.' Random I know, but let's go see if it's there.

Awesome! So, we know this works. Let's continue on to conencting this to our Linux server.

Create the Shared Directory

Now, create a directory wherever you like. This is directly that will point directly to your Google Drive. After the setup is complete, opening this will open your Google drive as if it was a folder on your server. So, let's do that here. For simplicity, give it the same name as your mount.

mkdir /home/YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_DIRECTORY_NAME

Now, we're going to edit a configuration file. This will allow Samba to see the mounted files. Start by entering this command:

sudo nano /etc/fuse.conf

After that, you should see a line that says "#user_allow_other." Remove the '#' to uncomment it. Save and close the file.

Great. Next we're going to make sure that Google Drive mounts everytime the server reboots. So we're first going to get our user id. You can get this by simply entering the id command in your terminal.

id YOUR_USERNAME

Good. Now we're going to create our systemmd service file. This is what will mount our Google Drive.

sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/rclone-gdrive.service

Once you're in the text editor, erase everything and enter this here replacing the following:

USERNAME: With your username

MOUNTNAME: With the name you gave your mount (mine was gdrive2)

UID / GUI: This was the ID you got earlier from the id command.

[Unit]
Description=Rclone Mount for Google Drive
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=USERNAME
Group=USERNAME
ExecStart=/usr/bin/rclone mount MOUNTNAME: /home/USERNAME/MOUNTNAME --config /home/USERNAME/.config/rclone/rclone.conf --allow-other --vfs-cache-mode writes --uid 1000 --gid 1000
ExecStop=/bin/fusermount -u /home/USERNAME/MOUNTNAME
Restart=always
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

Now apply the new configuration from the service file:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable rclone-gdrive.service
sudo systemctl start rclone-gdrive.service

Now the service should be started. Now let's make sure it's working by entering this command:

sudo systemctl status rclone-gdrive.service

You should see a green dot with an 'active' status indicating that the service is running:

Once you have that, Google Drive is mounted, and connected to the directory, ready to be shared on your network!

Mapping as a Network Drive

Glad to see you're still with me. The good news is the rest is fairly easy. Let's get Samba setup so we can use this as a network drive on your other computers.

We've already installed Samba, next let's edit the configuration file for Samba:

sudo nano /etc/samba/smb.conf

You're going to want to scroll down to the very bottom and add this block to the file. You're going to want to replace the path to your own, and the username to your own as well. This is mine as an example:

[GoogleDrive]
comment = Google Drive Shared Folder
path = /home/david/gdrive2
browseable = yes
read only = no
guest ok = no
valid users = david

Save and exit. Restart the Samba service:

sudo service smbd restart

Now, enter this command to allow Samba traffic:

sudo ufw allow samba

Create a username and password for Samba. Keep in mind, as you're typing the password, it will show up as blank but trust me, your keyboard is working, and you are typing a password.

sudo smbpasswd -a USERNAME

Mapping the Network Drive

Alright, the setup is finally done! Now we can map this directory, which points to your Google Drive, and map it on another computer on your network.

Now, on my Windows computer, if I type in my server's IP address, I should be able to see my shares, including the new one I just made.

Now, let't map it.

And there is my gdrive2 folder!

Conclusion

If you open it up, it should have your Google Drive files in it. Now I mainly use this locally, then when I'm remote I just use Google Drive's GUI since it's a bit faster but you may have a different experience depending on your server's performance.

I hope this was helpful and also clears up some storage space on your Linux server. If you have any questions, feel free to comment.
